title: Amines
note: An amine's lone pair makes it a base and a nucleophile. Compare base strength with the pKa of the conjugate ammonium ion: a higher pKa means a stronger base. Alkyl groups raise basicity; delocalizing the lone pair into a ring (aniline) or a carbonyl (amide) lowers it sharply.

read.title: The lone pair decides
text: Almost everything an amine does comes from the lone pair on nitrogen. It grabs protons, which makes amines the most common organic bases, and it attacks electrophiles, which makes amines good nucleophiles.

To compare base strength, chemists look at the conjugate acid. Methylammonium has a pKa near 10.6, a bit higher than ammonium's 9.3, because the methyl group pushes electron density onto nitrogen. Anilinium's pKa is only about 4.6. In aniline the lone pair is shared with the benzene ring, so it is less available for a proton. Amides go further: their lone pair is tied up with the carbonyl, and they are not protonated by dilute aqueous acid at all.

Making amines cleanly takes care. Ammonia and alkyl halides give mixtures, because each new amine is still nucleophilic and reacts again. Better routes build the C–N bond in a form that cannot overreact, then reduce it: azides, nitriles, and amides all become amines with LiAlH₄. Reductive amination joins a ketone or aldehyde to an amine and reduces the C=N in one pot. On aromatic rings, nitration followed by reduction gives anilines, and the diazonium salts made from them can be turned into halides, nitriles, and phenols.
